title: Validate Binary Search Tree
summary: Check that every node is strictly between the bounds set by its ancestors, not just bigger than its left child and smaller than its right child. Pass down an allowed range: going left tightens the upper bound, going right tightens the lower bound.
intuition: A BST constraint is global: everything in the left subtree must be smaller than the node.
Carry `(low, high)` down the recursion.
Use `long` bounds so nodes equal to Integer.MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE still work.
An in-order traversal must be strictly increasing; that's an equivalent check.
pitfalls: Only comparing a node with its direct children misses [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7].
Using int bounds with Integer.MIN_VALUE as -∞ fails when a node is exactly MIN_VALUE.
Allowing duplicates; this problem needs strict inequality.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
summary: An in-order traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order. Walk it iteratively with a stack: go left as far as possible, pop, count, then move right. The k-th popped node is the answer.

complexity.note: You can stop after k pops instead of traversing the whole tree.

intuition: In-order (left, node, right) on a BST is sorted ascending.
An explicit stack lets you stop early once k nodes are counted.
Push the whole left spine before popping.
pitfalls: Collecting all values into a list first is O(n) time and space.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
summary: In a BST, if both p and q are smaller than a node, their LCA is in the left subtree; if both are bigger, it's in the right subtree. The first node where they split (or that equals one of them) is the LCA.
intuition: The BST ordering tells you which side both nodes are on.
The split point, where p and q go different ways, is the lowest common ancestor.
A node can be its own ancestor: if p equals the current node, it's the answer.
pitfalls: Ignoring the BST property and using the general binary-tree solution (works, but misses the point).
Comparing node references instead of values when the inputs are values.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
summary: Search both subtrees for p and q. A node returns itself if it is p or q; otherwise it returns whatever its subtrees found. The first node that gets a non-null answer from both sides is the LCA.
intuition: Return value means "I found p, q, or their LCA in this subtree".
Both sides non-null: p and q are split here, so this node is the LCA.
One side non-null: pass that result up.
If the current node is p or q, return it immediately; the other can only be below it.
pitfalls: Assuming p and q are in different subtrees.
Searching each node separately with a contains() helper is O(n²).

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
summary: The first preorder value is the root. Finding it in the inorder array splits inorder into left and right subtrees, and the left part's size tells you how much of preorder belongs to the left subtree. Recurse on both parts; a map from value to inorder index keeps it O(n).

complexity.note: Each node is created once; the index map is O(n).

intuition: Preorder = root, left subtree, right subtree.
Inorder = left subtree, root, right subtree.
The root's inorder index splits the tree; `mid - inLo` is the left subtree size.
Consume preorder left to right with a single global index.
pitfalls: Searching inorder linearly every call is O(n²).
Building the right subtree before the left when using a running preorder index.
Values must be unique for the map to work.

Python.code:
def buildTree(preorder: List[int], inorder: List[int]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
    index = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}
    pre = 0

    def build(lo: int, hi: int) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        nonlocal pre
        if lo > hi: return None
        val = preorder[pre]
        pre += 1
        node = TreeNode(val)
        mid = index[val]
        node.left = build(lo, mid - 1)
        node.right = build(mid + 1, hi)
        return node

    return build(0, len(inorder) - 1)

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
summary: A path can bend at most once, at its highest node. For each node, compute the best downward path from it (`node + max(0, left, right)`) and, separately, the best path bending there (`node + left + right`, dropping negative sides). Track the best bend seen.
intuition: Return to the parent only a single downward branch, because a path can't fork twice.
Clamp negative branch sums to 0: skipping a branch is better than taking it.
Update the global answer with both branches at the current node.
Initialise the answer to the smallest int so all-negative trees work.
pitfalls: Initialising the best to 0 fails for trees with only negative values.
Returning `node + left + right` to the parent creates an invalid forked path.

Python.code:
def maxPathSum(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
    best = float("-inf")

    def gain(node: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        nonlocal best
        if not node: return 0
        left = max(0, gain(node.left))
        right = max(0, gain(node.right))
        best = max(best, node.val + left + right)
        return node.val + max(left, right)

    gain(root)
    return best

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
summary: Turn a tree into a string and back. Write a preorder traversal with `#` for null children; the markers make the shape unambiguous. To rebuild, read tokens in the same preorder: a number creates a node and recursively builds its left and right subtrees, `#` returns null.

complexity.note: Every node and null child is written and read once.

intuition: Preorder plus explicit nulls encodes the exact shape.
Deserialization mirrors serialization exactly: same order, same recursion.
A queue of tokens tracks the read position.
pitfalls: Leaving out null markers: [1, 2] and [1, null, 2] would serialize the same.
String concatenation in a loop is O(n²); use a StringBuilder.
Splitting on "," and forgetting negative numbers have a '-' sign (parseInt handles it).
